screens.title: Wallet Integration — MetaMask & WalletConnect
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on how a DApp securely connects to a user's wallet so it can request signatures and operate with a user identity. You will learn the role of a browser-injected provider like MetaMask's window. ethereum, how to request accounts using the standardized eth_requestAccounts call, and how to wrap that provider with an Ethers. js Web3Provider to obtain a signer for transactions. We'll also cover mobile wallet support using WalletConnect as a bridge, and the practical events you must listen for: accountsChanged and chainChanged. Those events require your DApp to update UI state or reinitialize contract connections to avoid inconsistent behavior. Along the way we'll emphasize UX constraints — like only requesting accounts in response to a clear user action — and error cases you should expect, for example when a user rejects a request or a chain is not added to their wallet. By the end you'll understand both the A P I calls and the user-facing patterns that make wallet integration robust and user friendly. Consider how these pieces work together: the wallet holds keys and signs; your DApp requests permission and adapts to the wallet's state. Ready to explore the specific steps and code patterns you will implement?

keyIdea.title: Why wallet integration matters
keyIdea.text: A wallet is the user's gatekeeper for identity and funds. Proper integration lets your DApp request signatures securely, reflect account and network state, and guide users to the correct network without exposing private keys.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Wallet Integration Overview
Wallet Integration — MetaMask & WalletConnect
In this lesson you will learn the APIs and UX patterns required to connect your DApp to browser and mobile wallets so users can sign transactions safely.
In this lesson
Detect window.ethereum, request accounts, wrap provider with Ethers.js.
Coming up
Handle accountsChanged and chainChanged. Support WalletConnect for mobile.
Why it matters
Good integration keeps user funds safe and prevents inconsistent app state when wallets change.
Visual concept
Browser Wallet
MetaMask injects window.ethereum → EIP-1193 provider
DApp
Requests eth_requestAccounts, wraps provider for Ethers.js signer
Mobile Wallets
WalletConnect bridges QR/deep links for signing
Key Takeaway

Treat the wallet as the authority for signing and chain identity. Detect provider, request user consent, and adapt to account or chain changes.

Terminal demo (concept)
// Example: request accounts & create provider
if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') {
  const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
  const provider = new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum);
  const signer = provider.getSigner();
  // listen for events: accountsChanged, chainChanged
}
Use this pattern inside a user-initiated action. For mobile support, integrate WalletConnect as a bridge that presents a QR or deep link to a mobile wallet.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical developer skills you will practice. First, you will be able to detect browser-injected providers like MetaMask and understand the EIP-1193 standard that governs them. Second, you will implement a secure connection flow that requests accounts only as a response to a user action and then wraps the provider with Ethers. js to obtain a signer for transaction signing. Third, you will handle the runtime events emitted by the wallet: accountsChanged and chainChanged, and learn how to update your UI and reinitialize contract connections accordingly. Finally, you will integrate WalletConnect to support mobile wallets and implement robust error handling for user rejections, missing chains, and provider disconnection. Each objective includes a concrete task and explains why it matters for reliable DApp behavior. These are practical, hands-on skills you will implement in the provided activity and use every time you build a production DApp.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide ties the developer tasks to user-facing outcomes you should test. Detecting window. ethereum prevents runtime errors when MetaMask is absent and enables graceful fallback messaging. Properly requesting accounts and wrapping the provider in Ethers. js ensures transactions are requested from the wallet rather than by your server, preserving user control of private keys. Handling accountsChanged ensures users who switch identities see updated balances and permissions immediately. Handling chainChanged or proactively calling wallet_switchEthereumChain lets you keep the DApp on the intended network such as Sepolia for development, and improves consistency. Integrating WalletConnect brings mobile users into the same signing model via a bridge, but adds lifecycle events like disconnect that you must handle. Finally, robust error handling for codes like 4001 (user rejected) and 4902 (chain not added) preserves UX and helps users recover. These outcomes are what you will validate in the hands-on activity and in QA before a release.

screens.title: What is window.ethereum and EIP-1193
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition. window. ethereum is the JavaScript object injected by browser wallets such as MetaMask that exposes methods for account access, sending requests, and emitting events. EIP-1193 standardizes how that provider behaves so DApps can rely on a consistent A P I across wallets. Practically, the provider provides methods like eth_requestAccounts and emits events such as accountsChanged and chainChanged. A concrete example: when your DApp calls the eth_requestAccounts method, MetaMask opens a prompt asking the user to connect; if the user approves, the wallet returns account addresses to your app. A common misconception is to treat window. ethereum as a safe place to read private data — it never contains private keys and never exposes signing material. Instead, consider it an RPC gateway and an event emitter. Another mistake is to assume it always exists; always check typeof window. ethereum!== 'undefined' to avoid runtime errors. This definition matters because recognizing the provider's role helps you design flows that respect user consent, avoid security pitfalls, and react to changing account or network state. So, when you detect the provider, think in terms of requesting permission, wrapping the provider with a library like Ethers. js, and listening to events so your app remains consistent with the wallet's view. How will you ensure your app never assumes a static account or network?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › What is window.ethereum
Definition
window.ethereum and EIP-1193
An injected provider that implements methods and events so your DApp can request accounts and listen for wallet state changes in a standardized way.
Example
Calling eth_requestAccounts triggers a wallet prompt; on approval the provider returns the connected accounts for your app to use.
Common misconception
window.ethereum does not expose private keys. It requests the wallet to sign on the user's behalf; never attempt to read keys from it.
Pitfall
Assuming window.ethereum always exists. Check typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined' before calling provider methods.
Key Takeaway

Treat the provider as a standardized bridge: request permission, let the wallet sign, and respond to events rather than assuming static state.

Terminal-style code sample
// Detection pattern
if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') {
  // Provider exists and implements EIP-1193
  const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
  // Use accounts[0] as the connected account
} else {
  // Prompt install guidance
}
This code encapsulates the definition: detect the injected provider, then request accounts under user control.

screens.title: Requesting Accounts & Creating a Signer
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the typical connection flow from user action to obtaining a signer. First, you detect the provider and then call eth_requestAccounts; this method should be invoked only after an explicit user action such as clicking a connect button. When the wallet prompts the user and the user approves, the wallet returns an array of accounts. Next, create an Ethers. js Web3Provider with the injected provider: new ethers. providers. Web3Provider(window. ethereum). Calling provider. getSigner returns a signer object that represents the currently selected account and allows your DApp to request transaction signatures without ever having access to private keys. A concrete example: a user clicks connect, MetaMask shows a prompt, they approve, and your UI displays accounts[0] and enables transaction buttons. A common mistake is trying to construct a Wallet from an address string; a wallet needs a private key and you must not attempt to recreate a signer from an address. Also avoid calling eth_requestAccounts on page load — it's intrusive and may be rejected. Closing takeaway: wrapping the injected provider with Ethers. js preserves the security model while giving you a developer-friendly interface for reading network info and requesting signatures. How will you ensure that eth_requestAccounts is always user-initiated in your app?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Request Accounts & Signer
Process
Request accounts and get a signer
Follow this user-initiated flow to obtain an Ethers.js signer without touching private keys.
1
Detect provider
Check typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined' before proceeding.
2
Request accounts
Call eth_requestAccounts in response to a gesture to trigger the wallet consent prompt.
3
Create provider & signer
new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum) then provider.getSigner() to request signatures.
Key Takeaway

Only request accounts after a clear user action and always use a provider wrapper like Ethers.js to request signing while keeping private keys in the wallet.

Code walkthrough
// Example flow (concept)
if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') {
  const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
  const provider = new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum);
  const signer = provider.getSigner();
  const userAddress = await signer.getAddress();
  // Use signer to request transaction signing
}
Do not create a Wallet from an address. A Wallet requires a private key and should never be constructed from a connected address in client code.

screens.title: Handling accountsChanged
screens.narratorSegment: Listening and responding to the accountsChanged event is essential for an accurate and secure DApp. The provider emits accountsChanged when the user switches their active account in MetaMask or disconnects all accounts. A typical handler receives the new accounts array. If the array is empty, treat this as a disconnection: clear any cached account state, update the UI to show the user is disconnected, and stop signing flows. If the array contains addresses, set the active account to the first entry and refresh account-specific data such as balances and allowance checks. A concrete example: a user switches from account A to account B; the handler updates the displayed address and reloads on-chain state tied to the active account. A common mistake is ignoring this event and continuing to show data tied to a stale account, which can lead to confusing UX or incorrect transaction context. Another pitfall is assuming only a single account exists: always handle arrays. Finally, for SPA architectures avoid full page reloads; reinitialize your provider, signer, and contract instances to preserve state while updating account-specific data. Closing question: how will you design your state model so that account changes trigger only the necessary updates rather than a full reload?

keyIdea.title: accountsChanged = update or disconnect
keyIdea.text: When accountsChanged fires, treat empty arrays as disconnects and non-empty arrays as a new active account; refresh account data and reinitialize relevant state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Handling accountsChanged
Event
accountsChanged
React to new account arrays by updating active account and refreshing account-specific data.
Empty array → disconnected
If newAccounts.length === 0, clear UI state and prevent signing flows until reconnected.
Non-empty → switch active account
Set the active account to newAccounts[0], refresh balances and contract reads that depend on the signer.
Misconception
Don't assume accounts won't change. Users switch accounts frequently for separation of concerns and testing.
Key Takeaway

Subscribe to accountsChanged and make account updates explicit: clear state on disconnects and refresh data on account switches.

Terminal-style handler
window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', (newAccounts) => {
  console.log('MetaMask accounts changed:', newAccounts);
  if (newAccounts.length === 0) {
    // handle logout / UI reset
  } else {
    // set active account to newAccounts[0] and refresh data
  }
});

screens.title: Handling chainChanged and network mismatches
screens.narratorSegment: Network changes require deliberate handling because contracts and addresses depend on chain identity. The chainChanged event fires when the user switches networks inside their wallet. When it occurs, you must re-initialize provider and contract connections or, in simple cases, reload the page. A concrete example: your DApp expects Sepolia for testing, but the user switches to Mainnet. Detect the mismatch by checking provider. getNetwork or eth_chainId, compare chainId to your target chain id — for Sepolia the chapter uses the hex 0xaa36a7 — and then call wallet_switchEthereumChain to request a network switch. If the chain is not added to the wallet, the provider can return error code 4902; handle that by prompting the user to add the chain using wallet_addEthereumChain, or show friendly instructions. Also handle user rejection via error code 4001. A common misconception is to ignore chain changes and proceed; this produces failed transactions or calls against missing contracts. Prefer to guide the user with clear messages, and avoid silent reloads in SPAs — instead reinitialize dependencies gracefully. Closing question: what strategy will you use to keep contract instances and caches in sync after a chain change?

keyIdea.text: On chainChanged, re-evaluate chainId, reinitialize provider and contract instances, and offer a switch using wallet_switchEthereumChain when appropriate.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Handling chainChanged
Definition
chainChanged
When the wallet switches networks, re-evaluate chain id and reinitialize blockchain connections to avoid inconsistent calls or failed transactions.
Check network
Use provider.getNetwork() or eth_chainId and compare to your expected chain id, e.g. Sepolia's 0xaa36a7 in hex.
Request switch
Call wallet_switchEthereumChain with the target chain id and handle errors like 4902 or user rejection 4001.
Misconception
Don't assume network never changes. Users may switch networks for testing or privacy; your app must handle it gracefully.
Why it matters

Contracts and RPC endpoints are chain-specific. A network mismatch can produce incorrect data or failed transactions; detecting and resolving it preserves correctness.

Example flow
window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', async (chainId) => {
  console.log('Network changed:', chainId);
  // Option: reload or reinitialize provider and contracts
  // Compare chainId to target (e.g. '0xaa36a7' for Sepolia) and call wallet_switchEthereumChain if needed
});

screens.title: Switching networks programmatically
screens.narratorSegment: When your DApp requires a specific network, you can programmatically ask the wallet to switch networks with wallet_switchEthereumChain. For example, to request Sepolia you would pass the hex chain id '0xaa36a7'. If the chain is not present in the wallet, the request can fail with code 4902, indicating the user must add the chain first using wallet_addEthereumChain. If the user rejects the prompt, you will receive error code 4001. A concrete example from the chapter shows catching these errors and prompting the user to add Sepolia or accept the switch. A common mistake is to assume a successful switch is guaranteed; always handle both user rejection and the missing-chain error and surface clear instructions. Another pitfall is reloading the page unconditionally — in single-page applications reinitialize the provider and contract instances instead of forcing a full reload when possible. Always present friendly UI messages that explain why the network matters and what the user must do. Closing thought: offering a clear one-click prompt to switch networks improves onboarding and reduces friction, but you must still handle the cases where the user declines or the chain is unknown.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Switching networks
API
wallet_switchEthereumChain
Request a wallet to switch to a provided chain id. If the chain is missing use wallet_addEthereumChain or show guidance.
Handle error 4902
4902 indicates the chain isn't added to the wallet. Offer to add the chain or explain manual steps.
Handle error 4001
4001 indicates the user rejected the request. Provide fallback instructions rather than retrying aggressively.
UX tip
Explain why you need the network and show clear steps so users understand what will change in their wallet.
Key Takeaway

Programmatic network switching improves reliability but requires careful error handling and user-friendly messaging for missing chains and rejections.

Code example (concept)
const sepoliaChainId = '0xaa36a7';
try {
  await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'wallet_switchEthereumChain', params: [{ chainId: sepoliaChainId }] });
} catch (switchError) {
  if (switchError.code === 4902) {
    // prompt to add chain
  } else if (switchError.code === 4001) {
    // user rejected
  }
}

screens.title: WalletConnect — mobile wallet bridging
screens.narratorSegment: WalletConnect provides a protocol-based bridge between web DApps and mobile wallets. Unlike MetaMask's injected provider which exists in the browser, WalletConnect relays messages between your DApp and a mobile wallet via a session that starts from a QR code or deep link. The bridge passes JSON-RPC messages so the mobile wallet can prompt the user to approve account connections and signature requests. A concrete example: a desktop user scans the QR code with their mobile wallet app; the WalletConnect provider then supplies accounts to your DApp and relays signing requests. One common misconception is that WalletConnect exposes private keys to the DApp — it does not. Signing still happens inside the mobile wallet. Another difference to note is lifecycle events: WalletConnect providers commonly emit accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect, so you must implement handlers similar to those used for injected providers. Also plan for provider disconnection and session termination so your UI returns to a disconnected state when the mobile wallet disconnects. In short, WalletConnect extends your DApp's reach to mobile users while keeping the same signing model and event-driven handling patterns you already use with window. ethereum. How will you test mobile flows alongside browser-based providers?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › WalletConnect
Definition
WalletConnect protocol
A bridge that connects web DApps to mobile wallets using QR codes or deep links to establish a signed session for JSON-RPC calls.
Concrete example
User scans a QR code, the session is established, and the wallet handles signing prompts on the mobile device.
Lifecycle events
WalletConnect providers support accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect. Handle them just as you would with an injected provider.
Security note
The private key stays in the mobile wallet. WalletConnect only relays the signing request and signed response.
Why it matters

WalletConnect expands your DApp's audience to mobile wallets without changing the signing model. Plan for session lifecycle handling and RPC configuration.

screens.title: MetaMask (injected) vs WalletConnect (bridge)
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing the two approaches clarifies integration choices. MetaMask's injected provider is simple for browser-based users: you detect window. ethereum and call eth_requestAccounts. It is lightweight with immediate provider access but limited to browsers where an extension is installed. WalletConnect is protocol-based and targets mobile wallets via QR or deep link; it requires an RPC configuration and a session lifecycle with connect and disconnect events. In both cases signing happens inside the wallet and you should never access private keys. A concrete contrast: with MetaMask you rely on the injected object and its events; with WalletConnect you initialize a provider client, display a QR code or deep link, and await session enablement. Both emit accountsChanged and chainChanged, but WalletConnect also often requires explicit handling for disconnect events when the mobile user terminates the session. A common misconception is that WalletConnect is more or less secure than an injected provider; security is equivalent at the signing level because keys remain in wallet apps. Choose injected when targeting desktop browser users and WalletConnect to cover mobile users; supporting both covers the widest audience. Closing question: which user scenarios in your app require both integrations to be available?

MetaMask (injected)
Detect window.ethereum, call eth_requestAccounts, wrap with Ethers.js Web3Provider. Best for desktop browser extension users.
Pros
Immediate provider access and simple event handling.

screens.title: Common mistakes and robust error handling
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson focuses on common integration mistakes and the error patterns you must handle. One frequent error is not checking for window. ethereum, which throws when MetaMask is missing. Another is calling eth_requestAccounts automatically on load; this can be intrusive and is often rejected by the user, returning error code 4001. When switching networks with wallet_switchEthereumChain you may encounter error code 4902 if the chain is not added to the wallet — handle this by prompting to add the chain via wallet_addEthereumChain or by showing clear instructions. WalletConnect sessions can disconnect; listen for disconnect and clear any session-dependent state. Do not construct signers from plain addresses; creating a Wallet from an address is meaningless without a private key. Always show user-friendly messages describing what failed and next steps. For example, when a user rejects connection, explain they can retry via the Connect action. A concrete recovery pattern: on failed switch with 4902, suggest adding the chain and offer a fallback to continue in read-only mode until the user adds the chain. Ending question: what recovery UI will you present when a critical wallet operation fails so users can proceed safely?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Common mistakes & errors
Common mistakes
  • Not checking for window.ethereum before calling provider methods.
  • Calling eth_requestAccounts on page load rather than on a user action.
  • Ignoring accountsChanged and chainChanged, leading to stale data.
  • Constructing a Wallet from an address instead of using the signer provided by the wallet.
Error codes to handle
4001: user rejected. 4902: chain not added. Also handle disconnect from WalletConnect provider.
Recovery patterns
On rejection show retry and explain why the permission matters. On 4902 present add-chain instructions or call wallet_addEthereumChain. On disconnect, clear state and prompt reconnect.
UX guideline

Keep messaging actionable: what the user must do, why, and what the result will be.

screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks through the index. html exercise provided in the chapter. The objective is to build a simple page that detects MetaMask, connects on user click, and displays the connected account and network. The flow is: create a Connect button that, when clicked, checks for typeof window. ethereum!== 'undefined'; if present, call eth_requestAccounts and display accounts[0] in the UI. After completing the activity, add a check for the expected chain id and attempt wallet_switchEthereumChain if there's a mismatch. What did you observe when switching accounts and chains during the test?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Activity: Connect & Monitor
Activity steps
  1. Create a Connect control that triggers a user action.
  2. Check for window.ethereum and call eth_requestAccounts on click.
  3. Wrap provider with new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum) and getSigner.
  4. Display accounts[0], network name, and chain id.

Key result

By following these steps you will observe real-time updates as the wallet state changes and learn how to make the UI resilient to those changes.

Starter code (index.html excerpt)
// On Connect click
const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
provider = new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum);
signer = provider.getSigner();
const network = await provider.getNetwork();
// Set up listeners
window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', handleAccountsChanged);
window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', handleChainChanged);

screens.title: Provider-wrapper architecture with Ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a clear provider-wrapper architecture helps you handle wallet lifecycle events and reduce bugs. The recommended structure places the injected provider or WalletConnect provider at the top level, which you immediately wrap with new ethers. providers. Web3Provider(provider). From that wrapper you derive a signer with provider. getSigner and create contract instances with new ethers. Contract(address, abi, signer). Keep a small initialization module that exports the current provider, signer, and contract instances so other parts of the app can import them. When accountsChanged or chainChanged fires, update the signer and reinstantiate contract objects. A concrete pattern: maintain a reactive state object with fields for provider, signer, userAddress, and network; when events occur, update those fields and run a reinitContracts function that recreates contract instances with the new signer. A common mistake is to reuse a signer tied to a stale account; that leads to transactions being requested for the wrong account. Another pitfall is holding contract instances across network changes; always recreate them after a chain change. This architecture keeps responsibility clear: wallet provider is the source of truth for signing and chain identity, and your app's contract layer is rebuilt when the provider's context changes. How will you structure your initialization so reinitialization is safe and minimal?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Provider-wrapper architecture
Initialization pattern
Keep a small module that provides provider, signer, and contract instances. Recreate contracts when the provider context changes.
State model
Track provider, signer, userAddress, and network. Use these fields to decide which UI components to enable.
Reinit strategy
On accountsChanged or chainChanged run a reinit function that recreates signer and contract objects to avoid stale references.
Key Takeaway

Centralize provider initialization and reinstantiate contracts on provider changes so the rest of your app can rely on fresh signer-bound contract instances.

Architecture sketch
Provider (MetaMask / WalletConnect) → Web3Provider → Signer → Contract instances Reinitialize contracts when provider or signer changes to ensure transaction requests use the current account and network.

screens.title: Assessment: choosing the correct signer pattern
screens.narratorSegment: This slide explains the assessment idea from the chapter and how to reason through the options. The correct secure approach after a user clicks Connect is to create a Web3Provider from window. ethereum and then call provider. getSigner to obtain a signer that represents the wallet's active account. This pattern uses the injected provider for signing requests while keeping the private key inside the wallet. Contrast that with incorrect options: using a JsonRpcProvider pointed at a local RPC does not leverage the user's MetaMask signing session, and trying to construct a Wallet from a public address is invalid because a Wallet requires a private key. Another wrong approach is to use window. ethereum. selectedAddress to craft a Wallet; selectedAddress might be unavailable and does not give you signing capabilities. The recommended path is: eth_requestAccounts → new ethers. providers. Web3Provider(window. ethereum) → provider. getSigner. Practically, this means you call eth_requestAccounts in response to the user's click, then create the signer and request transaction signatures via signer methods. Final reflection: how does this pattern preserve user control of private keys while allowing your DApp to request transactions?

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on how a DApp securely connects to a user's wallet so it can request signatures and operate with a user identity. You will learn the role of a browser-injected provider like MetaMask's window. ethereum, how to request accounts using the standardized eth_requestAccounts call, and how to wrap that provider with an Ethers. js Web3Provider to obtain a signer for transactions. We'll also cover mobile wallet support using WalletConnect as a bridge, and the practical events you must listen for: accountsChanged and chainChanged. Those events require your DApp to update UI state or reinitialize contract connections to avoid inconsistent behavior. Along the way we'll emphasize UX constraints — like only requesting accounts in response to a clear user action — and error cases you should expect, for example when a user rejects a request or a chain is not added to their wallet. By the end you'll understand both the A P I calls and the user-facing patterns that make wallet integration robust and user friendly. Consider how these pieces work together: the wallet holds keys and signs; your DApp requests permission and adapts to the wallet's state. Ready to explore the specific steps and code patterns you will implement?

These learning objectives map to practical developer skills you will practice. First, you will be able to detect browser-injected providers like MetaMask and understand the EIP-1193 standard that governs them. Second, you will implement a secure connection flow that requests accounts only as a response to a user action and then wraps the provider with Ethers. js to obtain a signer for transaction signing. Third, you will handle the runtime events emitted by the wallet: accountsChanged and chainChanged, and learn how to update your UI and reinitialize contract connections accordingly. Finally, you will integrate WalletConnect to support mobile wallets and implement robust error handling for user rejections, missing chains, and provider disconnection. Each objective includes a concrete task and explains why it matters for reliable DApp behavior. These are practical, hands-on skills you will implement in the provided activity and use every time you build a production DApp.

This second objectives slide ties the developer tasks to user-facing outcomes you should test. Detecting window. ethereum prevents runtime errors when MetaMask is absent and enables graceful fallback messaging. Properly requesting accounts and wrapping the provider in Ethers. js ensures transactions are requested from the wallet rather than by your server, preserving user control of private keys. Handling accountsChanged ensures users who switch identities see updated balances and permissions immediately. Handling chainChanged or proactively calling wallet_switchEthereumChain lets you keep the DApp on the intended network such as Sepolia for development, and improves consistency. Integrating WalletConnect brings mobile users into the same signing model via a bridge, but adds lifecycle events like disconnect that you must handle. Finally, robust error handling for codes like 4001 (user rejected) and 4902 (chain not added) preserves UX and helps users recover. These outcomes are what you will validate in the hands-on activity and in QA before a release.

Start with a clear definition. window. ethereum is the JavaScript object injected by browser wallets such as MetaMask that exposes methods for account access, sending requests, and emitting events. EIP-1193 standardizes how that provider behaves so DApps can rely on a consistent A P I across wallets. Practically, the provider provides methods like eth_requestAccounts and emits events such as accountsChanged and chainChanged. A concrete example: when your DApp calls the eth_requestAccounts method, MetaMask opens a prompt asking the user to connect; if the user approves, the wallet returns account addresses to your app. A common misconception is to treat window. ethereum as a safe place to read private data — it never contains private keys and never exposes signing material. Instead, consider it an RPC gateway and an event emitter. Another mistake is to assume it always exists; always check typeof window. ethereum!== 'undefined' to avoid runtime errors. This definition matters because recognizing the provider's role helps you design flows that respect user consent, avoid security pitfalls, and react to changing account or network state. So, when you detect the provider, think in terms of requesting permission, wrapping the provider with a library like Ethers. js, and listening to events so your app remains consistent with the wallet's view. How will you ensure your app never assumes a static account or network?

This lesson walks through the typical connection flow from user action to obtaining a signer. First, you detect the provider and then call eth_requestAccounts; this method should be invoked only after an explicit user action such as clicking a connect button. When the wallet prompts the user and the user approves, the wallet returns an array of accounts. Next, create an Ethers. js Web3Provider with the injected provider: new ethers. providers. Web3Provider(window. ethereum). Calling provider. getSigner returns a signer object that represents the currently selected account and allows your DApp to request transaction signatures without ever having access to private keys. A concrete example: a user clicks connect, MetaMask shows a prompt, they approve, and your UI displays accounts[0] and enables transaction buttons. A common mistake is trying to construct a Wallet from an address string; a wallet needs a private key and you must not attempt to recreate a signer from an address. Also avoid calling eth_requestAccounts on page load — it's intrusive and may be rejected. Closing takeaway: wrapping the injected provider with Ethers. js preserves the security model while giving you a developer-friendly interface for reading network info and requesting signatures. How will you ensure that eth_requestAccounts is always user-initiated in your app?

Listening and responding to the accountsChanged event is essential for an accurate and secure DApp. The provider emits accountsChanged when the user switches their active account in MetaMask or disconnects all accounts. A typical handler receives the new accounts array. If the array is empty, treat this as a disconnection: clear any cached account state, update the UI to show the user is disconnected, and stop signing flows. If the array contains addresses, set the active account to the first entry and refresh account-specific data such as balances and allowance checks. A concrete example: a user switches from account A to account B; the handler updates the displayed address and reloads on-chain state tied to the active account. A common mistake is ignoring this event and continuing to show data tied to a stale account, which can lead to confusing UX or incorrect transaction context. Another pitfall is assuming only a single account exists: always handle arrays. Finally, for SPA architectures avoid full page reloads; reinitialize your provider, signer, and contract instances to preserve state while updating account-specific data. Closing question: how will you design your state model so that account changes trigger only the necessary updates rather than a full reload?

Network changes require deliberate handling because contracts and addresses depend on chain identity. The chainChanged event fires when the user switches networks inside their wallet. When it occurs, you must re-initialize provider and contract connections or, in simple cases, reload the page. A concrete example: your DApp expects Sepolia for testing, but the user switches to Mainnet. Detect the mismatch by checking provider. getNetwork or eth_chainId, compare chainId to your target chain id — for Sepolia the chapter uses the hex 0xaa36a7 — and then call wallet_switchEthereumChain to request a network switch. If the chain is not added to the wallet, the provider can return error code 4902; handle that by prompting the user to add the chain using wallet_addEthereumChain, or show friendly instructions. Also handle user rejection via error code 4001. A common misconception is to ignore chain changes and proceed; this produces failed transactions or calls against missing contracts. Prefer to guide the user with clear messages, and avoid silent reloads in SPAs — instead reinitialize dependencies gracefully. Closing question: what strategy will you use to keep contract instances and caches in sync after a chain change?

When your DApp requires a specific network, you can programmatically ask the wallet to switch networks with wallet_switchEthereumChain. For example, to request Sepolia you would pass the hex chain id '0xaa36a7'. If the chain is not present in the wallet, the request can fail with code 4902, indicating the user must add the chain first using wallet_addEthereumChain. If the user rejects the prompt, you will receive error code 4001. A concrete example from the chapter shows catching these errors and prompting the user to add Sepolia or accept the switch. A common mistake is to assume a successful switch is guaranteed; always handle both user rejection and the missing-chain error and surface clear instructions. Another pitfall is reloading the page unconditionally — in single-page applications reinitialize the provider and contract instances instead of forcing a full reload when possible. Always present friendly UI messages that explain why the network matters and what the user must do. Closing thought: offering a clear one-click prompt to switch networks improves onboarding and reduces friction, but you must still handle the cases where the user declines or the chain is unknown.

WalletConnect provides a protocol-based bridge between web DApps and mobile wallets. Unlike MetaMask's injected provider which exists in the browser, WalletConnect relays messages between your DApp and a mobile wallet via a session that starts from a QR code or deep link. The bridge passes JSON-RPC messages so the mobile wallet can prompt the user to approve account connections and signature requests. A concrete example: a desktop user scans the QR code with their mobile wallet app; the WalletConnect provider then supplies accounts to your DApp and relays signing requests. One common misconception is that WalletConnect exposes private keys to the DApp — it does not. Signing still happens inside the mobile wallet. Another difference to note is lifecycle events: WalletConnect providers commonly emit accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect, so you must implement handlers similar to those used for injected providers. Also plan for provider disconnection and session termination so your UI returns to a disconnected state when the mobile wallet disconnects. In short, WalletConnect extends your DApp's reach to mobile users while keeping the same signing model and event-driven handling patterns you already use with window. ethereum. How will you test mobile flows alongside browser-based providers?

Comparing the two approaches clarifies integration choices. MetaMask's injected provider is simple for browser-based users: you detect window. ethereum and call eth_requestAccounts. It is lightweight with immediate provider access but limited to browsers where an extension is installed. WalletConnect is protocol-based and targets mobile wallets via QR or deep link; it requires an RPC configuration and a session lifecycle with connect and disconnect events. In both cases signing happens inside the wallet and you should never access private keys. A concrete contrast: with MetaMask you rely on the injected object and its events; with WalletConnect you initialize a provider client, display a QR code or deep link, and await session enablement. Both emit accountsChanged and chainChanged, but WalletConnect also often requires explicit handling for disconnect events when the mobile user terminates the session. A common misconception is that WalletConnect is more or less secure than an injected provider; security is equivalent at the signing level because keys remain in wallet apps. Choose injected when targeting desktop browser users and WalletConnect to cover mobile users; supporting both covers the widest audience. Closing question: which user scenarios in your app require both integrations to be available?

This lesson focuses on common integration mistakes and the error patterns you must handle. One frequent error is not checking for window. ethereum, which throws when MetaMask is missing. Another is calling eth_requestAccounts automatically on load; this can be intrusive and is often rejected by the user, returning error code 4001. When switching networks with wallet_switchEthereumChain you may encounter error code 4902 if the chain is not added to the wallet — handle this by prompting to add the chain via wallet_addEthereumChain or by showing clear instructions. WalletConnect sessions can disconnect; listen for disconnect and clear any session-dependent state. Do not construct signers from plain addresses; creating a Wallet from an address is meaningless without a private key. Always show user-friendly messages describing what failed and next steps. For example, when a user rejects connection, explain they can retry via the Connect action. A concrete recovery pattern: on failed switch with 4902, suggest adding the chain and offer a fallback to continue in read-only mode until the user adds the chain. Ending question: what recovery UI will you present when a critical wallet operation fails so users can proceed safely?

Designing a clear provider-wrapper architecture helps you handle wallet lifecycle events and reduce bugs. The recommended structure places the injected provider or WalletConnect provider at the top level, which you immediately wrap with new ethers. providers. Web3Provider(provider). From that wrapper you derive a signer with provider. getSigner and create contract instances with new ethers. Contract(address, abi, signer). Keep a small initialization module that exports the current provider, signer, and contract instances so other parts of the app can import them. When accountsChanged or chainChanged fires, update the signer and reinstantiate contract objects. A concrete pattern: maintain a reactive state object with fields for provider, signer, userAddress, and network; when events occur, update those fields and run a reinitContracts function that recreates contract instances with the new signer. A common mistake is to reuse a signer tied to a stale account; that leads to transactions being requested for the wrong account. Another pitfall is holding contract instances across network changes; always recreate them after a chain change. This architecture keeps responsibility clear: wallet provider is the source of truth for signing and chain identity, and your app's contract layer is rebuilt when the provider's context changes. How will you structure your initialization so reinitialization is safe and minimal?

This slide explains the assessment idea from the chapter and how to reason through the options. The correct secure approach after a user clicks Connect is to create a Web3Provider from window. ethereum and then call provider. getSigner to obtain a signer that represents the wallet's active account. This pattern uses the injected provider for signing requests while keeping the private key inside the wallet. Contrast that with incorrect options: using a JsonRpcProvider pointed at a local RPC does not leverage the user's MetaMask signing session, and trying to construct a Wallet from a public address is invalid because a Wallet requires a private key. Another wrong approach is to use window. ethereum. selectedAddress to craft a Wallet; selectedAddress might be unavailable and does not give you signing capabilities. The recommended path is: eth_requestAccounts → new ethers. providers. Web3Provider(window. ethereum) → provider. getSigner. Practically, this means you call eth_requestAccounts in response to the user's click, then create the signer and request transaction signatures via signer methods. Final reflection: how does this pattern preserve user control of private keys while allowing your DApp to request transactions?

These three core concepts summarize the chapter. First, window. ethereum is the injected provider that adheres to EIP-1193; use it as the gateway to request accounts and listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged events. Second, always trigger eth_requestAccounts from a user gesture, then wrap the injected provider with Ethers. js Web3Provider and obtain a signer via provider. getSigner so signing occurs within the wallet. Third, WalletConnect is a protocol bridge that extends signing to mobile wallets using QR codes or deep links; it preserves the signing model but adds session lifecycle events like disconnect which you must handle. Keep these ideas in mind as you implement connection flows and design user-friendly error recovery. How will you apply them in your next DApp?
